title: A region before and after a map: how are areas and shapes changed?
summary: A coloured region in the (u, v) plane on the left, its image under a map on the right, with the same colouring on both sides. The Jacobian determinant tells you by what factor small areas were scaled and whether orientation was kept.

media.alt: Left: a unit square coloured by u from purple to yellow with a thin grid and an orange outline. Right: the same square bent by a map into a curved region with the same colouring, grid lines and outline, and a text box giving the range of the Jacobian determinant.
media.caption: Reference render of class F2.1 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data. Standard theory only.

read_the_figure.question: How are areas and shapes changed?
read_the_figure.axes: Left (domain D): u horizontal and v vertical, both 0 to 1. Right (image F(D)): x and y, equal scale. Colour is u on both sides and one colour bar serves both. The orange line is the boundary of the region.
look_at: Follow one colour band from left to right: where does the band for u = 0.5 end up?
Do grid cells keep their order and handedness, or do any fold over? Orientation kept means no fold.
Where do cells grow and where do they shrink? Look at the top-right tip and the middle of the right edge.
Does the printed determinant range stay above zero?
as_drawn: The domain has area 1. The text says det J lies in [0.30, 1.56], positive everywhere, and quotes an image area of 0.97 as the mean of det J on the sample grid.
The exact mean of det J is 0.9775 (the area of the image), so the printed 0.97 is a sampling effect: the grid mean is a rough estimate.
Same colouring on both sides is satisfied: the colour bar says 'colour = u (same on both sides)'.
read_the_figure.proves: That the map keeps orientation (det J > 0) and by how much it scales small areas. A mean close to 1 does NOT mean areas are preserved locally: the local factor here runs from 0.3 to 1.6.
if_wrong: Different colouring on the two sides: you cannot match points.
A map that folds drawn with a solid fill: the overlap hides the fold.
Image drawn with unequal axis scales: areas and angles are misjudged.

terms.meaning: A rule that sends each point (u, v) of a region to a point (x, y).
The region before the map, D, and the region after, F(D).
The matrix of all first partial derivatives of the map: the best linear approximation near a point.
The factor by which the map scales small areas. Negative means orientation is reversed.
Whether the sense u-then-v (counter-clockwise) is kept after the map.
The rule that an area or integral in the image equals the integral over the domain of |det J|.

remember: Image area = integral of |det J| over the domain.
det J > 0: orientation kept. det J < 0: flipped. det J = 0: squashed to a curve or point (singular).
Same colouring on both sides is what lets you track points.
Equal axis scales on both panels.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Position on each side is the plane. Colour is the value of u, repeated on both panels, so a colour names a point set that you can follow through the map. The orange outline marks the boundary, the thin dark grid shows coordinate lines. The text box gives the number: det J.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: A map can be hard to see from a formula. Drawing a simple region, here a square, before and after lets you see the bend and the stretch. Colour carries identity across the map, so you can say exactly where each part of the original went. The Jacobian determinant turns the visual impression of 'bigger or smaller' into a number: the local area factor.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: Eyeballing area is unreliable, especially for curved shapes. A mean determinant near 1 hides local growth and shrinkage. If the map folds, the image overlaps itself and a filled picture hides it. And the colour channel, being a single scalar field, cannot show both the u and the v coordinate.

understand.title: Why each required item matters
understand.text: The same colouring on both sides is what makes 'before and after' a comparison and not two pictures. The Jacobian note is the quantitative statement: without it the reader has only the impression of growth or shrinkage.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A determinant heat map (F2.3) shows where the scale factor lives and where the map is singular. A deformed grid (F2.2) shows the coordinate lines without a fill. For a small displacement, a vector field of x - u is clearer. For a linear map, a unit square to a parallelogram is enough.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Colour the left panel by v and the right by u + v in a second figure so both coordinates are tracked. Overlay a small circle on the left and its image ellipse on the right to show the local stretch.

steps.title: The Jacobian determinant of the map
steps.note: A 2-by-2 determinant of the four partial derivatives. At (u, v) = (1, 1) it is 0.30 (the narrow tip); at (1, 0.5) it is 1.56 (the widest part of the right edge). The render's range [0.30, 1.56] matches.

steps.title: Area of the image
steps.note: The cosine term integrates to zero over a full period. A boundary integral (Green's theorem) on the image's outline gives the same 0.9775. The picture's 0.97 is the average of 3,600 samples, slightly off.

worked.title: Reading the reference render
worked.problem: From the figure: (1) is orientation kept? (2) Where does the map shrink area most and where does it grow it most? (3) What is the area of the image and is it close to 1 everywhere?

solution.text: The colours still go from dark on the left to bright on the right and the grid cells keep their handedness; the text says det J > 0 everywhere, so no flip.
The top-right corner is a narrow tip (det J about 0.30, shrunk by a factor of 3), the middle of the right edge is wide (det J about 1.56).

The image area equals the average of det J, 0.98 (the picture's printed 0.97 is a sampling estimate). The total is near 1 but local factors range over a factor of five, so the map is far from area-preserving.

worked.answer: Orientation kept; shrink at the top-right tip (0.30), growth in the middle of the right edge (1.56); total area 0.98, which hides a fivefold local variation.

analyze.q: Why can a mean det J of 1 coexist with a map that squeezes the top-right corner by a factor of three?
analyze.hint: A mean is a sum of local contributions that can cancel.

analyze.q: How would the picture change if det J became negative in a patch?
analyze.hint: Think of a fold-over of the colours.

analyze.q: What extra element would you add so the reader can read the shape change of a small circle?

evaluate.q: A paper says a deformation 'preserves volume' because the mean Jacobian is 1.00. Is that enough?

create: Draw a map with a fold (det J < 0 in a patch) and show how the same colouring exposes it.
Add the contour det J = 1 on the image panel to separate growth from shrinkage.

checks.q: What does det J > 0 tell you about the map?
checks.answer: The map keeps orientation: no reflection or fold. Small areas are scaled by det J.

checks.q: A small square of area 0.01 sits where det J = 1.5. What is its image area?
The image of a region looks bigger than the region. Does that prove det J > 1 everywhere?
checks.answer: No: it shows the average factor is above 1. The determinant can be below 1 in places, which is why the local value is needed.
